item.title: The Leonida Report, Ep 1: Thirty-Two Million and a Gator
item.description:
• Big One, the official number (Hot): Take-Two reports 32.5M units sold through launch day and an estimated $3.79B in revenue, which it calls a one-day record for entertainment in any medium. That is about three times GTA V's day one (11M, $800M, per Niko Partners' Daniel Ahmad) and tops Avengers: Endgame's lifetime box office ($2.94B, per Kotaku). Sensor Tower's 24.58M estimate came in about 8M short.
  • Big One, the review bomb (Pip: Not; Alder dissents: Lukewarm): Critics still at 99. The PS5 user score swung between 3.7 and 5.6 over two days; GTABase's Nov 21 reading is 5.6 from about 67.7K ratings, split 49% positive and 44% negative. It is also caught up in a zero-score war with the Ocarina of Time remake. The PlayStation Store, where only owners can rate, shows 4.84/5 (Dexerto).
  • Big One, cut side activities (Not): fans online are calling the removed sex-work and cheating features "woke." Rockstar told Shacknews the game is about a couple on the run, and features that didn't fit that story were cut.
  • Big One, The Game Awards (Hot): VGC reports GTA VI is the most nominated game of TGA 2026, which clears our corrections queue.
  • Review Roundup: Metacritic 99 from about 152 critics; OpenCritic 99. Ocarina's 99 came from 22 critics. Highlights: PC Gamer's roundup ("magnum opus") and GameSpot's haystack of needles. Slant's 4.5/5 is the "pan." Critics and angry users point at the same three faults: 30fps, slow pacing and realism friction.
  • By the Stats: GTA V's whole first month was about 29M (Motley Fool). Wedbush's 30 to 40M by year end was passed on day one; Wells Fargo projects 65M by Mar 31, 2027. Take-Two guides FY27 net bookings at $8B to $8.2B. TTWO closed at $210.00 on Nov 20 (+0.65%), down about 18.5% YTD. Morgan Stanley's target is $280; the median of 31 analysts is about $290. Guinness puts preorders near $750M, still being verified.
  • Editorial Desk: Kotaku's "Why Should I Care About GTA 6?" (the world or the story?), Creative Bloq's "graphics might be too good" (it aged well, says Alder), the Motley Fool's bull case (a labeled stock pitch), and Pip's own case that the slow opening is a strength.
  • Streamer Watch: Streams Charts recorded peaks of 3.31M on Twitch (the platform's game record), 3.21M on YouTube and 1.5M on Kick, plus a Kick record of 1,798 channels streaming at once. Personal peaks: IlloJuan, Windah Basudara, alanzoka, PAULINHO O LOKO and rraenee. No verified speedrun leaderboard yet.
  • Fan Pulse: Red Dead shared-universe clues (Kotaku, GameRoll; unconfirmed). No patch since 01.002.001 on Nov 16; the "Nov 25 fix" is an unverified social post. A plagiarism-claim headline we could not verify.
  • Hands-On: Alder has logged 22 hours and car repairs top his expenses. Pip is at 14 hours with three story missions done, and Gerald the gator beat him for the fifth time.
  • Statement Autopsy: we checked Take-Two's "biggest entertainment launch" release. The units are solid, the dollars are the company's estimate, and the record is real but measures revenue, not reach. The gap is small.
  • Speed Round: GTA VI: The Festival at Mana Wynwood (Nov 21), Bryan Mbeumo's "Historic" post, no PC date, no new patch, and the code-in-box edition.
  • Corrections: the sales figure is now official, Sensor Tower undercounted, and the GOTY nomination is confirmed. Prediction receipts: official number by Nov 30 (both right), first-week sales over 20M (both right), user score under 8.0 (Alder right). Odds updated on the open calls.

  • Hands-on (spoiler-safe): the information-based wanted system and six stars, repair costs, the radio satire, the drywall and "Sims" debate, and Pip's new nemesis, Gerald the gas station gator.

  • Money: Take-Two has published no sales number. Sensor Tower's day-one estimate climbed from 17.1M to 19.1M to about 24.6M copies (~$2.36B). item.title: The Weyland Files, Part 27: The Grand Map
item.description:
The finale. Pip and Alder put all twenty-six previous parts on one timeline, from the Engineers seeding life to Alien Resurrection around 2380 and Badlands beyond it. They then work through the threads (the companies, synthetics vs. replicants, the Engineers, the Yautja and the real-world rights holders) and close with a verdict board that labels every link CANON, CREATOR COMMENT, WINK or FAN THEORY. Alder's long-running Aliens/Blade Runner thesis ends "vindicated in spirit, defeated on paper."

  • Deep past: The Engineers seed life (Prometheus, CANON); ancient Yautja visits and a 100-year hunt cycle (AVP, CANON for Predator, contested for Alien); Lovecraft as the root of the theme.
  • Predator line: 841, 1609, 1715 (the Adolini pistol), 1719, 1904, 1942, 1987, 1997, 2004, The Predator (between 1997 and Predators), Predators (~2010), Badlands (well into the future), plus the undated Warehouse.
  • Blade Runner line: 2019, the Nexus-8 (2020), the Blackout (2022), Black Lotus (2032), Nexus Dawn (2036), 2048, 2049, and Blade Runner 2099 (Prime Video, scheduled for 2027).
  • Alien line: Weyland Corp (2012), the TED talk (2023), Prometheus (2093), Covenant (2104), Alien: Earth (2120), Alien (2122, tie-in year), Romulus (2142), Aliens/Alien 3 (2179), Resurrection (~2380).
  • Companies: Weyland Industries, Weyland Corp, Yutani, Weyland-Yutani, Hyperdyne, Prodigy, Lynch, Dynamic, Threshold, Tyrell, Wallace and Tian. The merger date is still unpinned (FAN THEORY). The Tyrell-Weyland bridge rests on a DVD dossier (tie-in), a Blu-ray in-joke (WINK) and Ridley's musings (CREATOR COMMENT).
  • Synthetics vs. replicants: Built (white fluid) vs. grown (red blood). Alien: Earth lists cyborgs, synthetics and hybrids, with no replicants. That the two technologies are related is FAN THEORY; as a theme they are one evolving idea.
  • Engineers: The Space Jockey retcon and black goo are CANON. Romulus's Z-01 ties back to Prometheus, while Hawley calls the bioweapon origin "less useful" (CREATOR COMMENT clash). The Guzikowski film may bring the prequel line back.
  • Yautja: Centuries of visits, an honor code, xeno hunting, a collecting civilization (the Warehouse), and Badlands' Weyland-Yutani synthetics as the second on-screen fusion point after the Predator 2 skull (CANON). Trachtenberg: "we just took Weyland-Yutani... the synths."
  • Real-world rights: Disney/20th Century owns Alien and Predator; Alcon controls Blade Runner. Mergers shelved, cancelled or wrote off several entries along the way.
  • Verdict board: Alien-Predator is CANON. Alien-Blade Runner is not canon (WINKS plus CREATOR COMMENT; about 3% by Alder's estimate). Soldier: CREATOR COMMENT/WINK. Event Horizon: FAN THEORY. Underwater: WINK. Raised by Wolves: creators say no. Deckard: unresolved.
  • Craft and theme pins: Ridley and Luke Scott, Wolski, Mead, Cobb, Winston/ADI/Legacy, Henriksen, Ian Whyte, Henwick, Biehn, Wallfisch; cosmic horror, makers and the made, corporate dystopia, the hunt as recognition.
  • Map update: The final board has solid Alien, Predator and Blade Runner lines; two Alien-Predator fusion points; a dotted Alien-Blade Runner line; dotted edge cases; the Easter egg drawer; Alder's probability estimates (opinion, not fact).
  • Unverified: The W-Y merger date, Badlands' exact year, on-screen confirmation of 2122/2179, 2099's release, the Guzikowski film's contents, Alien: Earth S2 timing, and the Warehouse payoff.

item.title: The Weyland Files, Part 26: Blade Runner 2099
item.description:
A "what we know" episode. Recorded November 16, 2026, before Blade Runner 2099 premieres on Prime Video on November 25, 2026, when all eight episodes come out at once. Pip and Alder cover the show's production history, cast, premise and creative aims, how it might fit the timeline, and some pre-release predictions with stated odds. There is no review, because nobody has seen it yet.

  • Status: Not yet released. Amazon MGM Studios set the premiere for November 25, 2026, in 240+ countries and territories, with 8 episodes. Wikipedia's article on the series still says 2027, which is out of date.
  • Development: Ridley Scott told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that a pilot and series bible had been written, in the same interview where he described the Alien series. Amazon put the show into development in February 2022 (Deadline) and ordered it as a limited series in September 2022.
  • Directors: Jeremy Podeswa was hired to direct in March 2023 and left in February 2024 after the strikes. Jonathan van Tulleken (Shōgun) directs episodes 1 and 2.
  • Locations: Filming was planned for Belfast but the 2023 WGA strike postponed it, and the production then left Northern Ireland. Filming took place in Prague from May/June 2024 and wrapped in December 2024.
  • Cast: Michelle Yeoh plays Olwen, a dying replicant Blade Runner. Hunter Schafer plays Cora, a human fugitive posing as a Blade Runner. Also starring Dimitri Abold, Lewis Gribben, Tom Burke and Sheila Atim. Hugo Hamlet plays Buster Friendly, a character from the novel.
  • Premise: Set 50 years after 2049. According to showrunner Silka Luisa (speaking to EW), replicants won the war and humans are now second-class citizens (CREATOR COMMENT).
  • Roy Batty model: Luisa says Olwen's story takes Roy Batty's arc from the first film and tells it from the replicant's side.
  • "Sunshine noir": Luisa told Empire the show has a hot, sticky, chaotic Los Angeles rather than rain and night.
  • Standalone: Luisa told SFX that the show isn't directly connected to 2049, and that Deckard, K and Ana Stelline don't appear.
  • Philip K. Dick: The writers went back to Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? for world-building. Isa Dick Hackett is an executive producer.
  • Scott-verse thread: Scott is an executive producer on both 2099 and Alien: Earth. Michael Green co-wrote 2049, shares a story credit on Alien: Covenant, and is an executive producer here. That's an overlap of creators, not a shared-universe claim.
  • Predictions: Spinners 90%, Voight-Kampff 90%, Wallace Corp mentioned 60%, a tears-in-rain echo 70%, a Weyland-Yutani Easter egg 3% (all FAN THEORY guesses).
  • Map update (provisional): 2049 to 2099, the replicant uprising wins. In 2099 Los Angeles is "reborn, just not by humanity", and replicant Blade Runners hunt rogue replicants. Replicant lifespans are longer but finite. This is the furthest-forward Blade Runner pin, 21 years before Alien: Earth.

item.title: The Weyland Files, Part 25: Predator: Badlands (2025)
item.description:
The company finally shows up. Pip and Alder take on Predator: Badlands (2025), Dan Trachtenberg and Patrick Aison's PG-13, Predator-as-hero adventure. Dek, a runt Yautja, hunts the unkillable Kalisk on the death planet Genna with Thia, half of a Weyland-Yutani synthetic (Elle Fanning, who also plays her villainous "sister" Tessa). The hosts go through every Weyland-Yutani connection with labels, place the film on the far-future timeline, and look at the box office record, the reception, and the crossover question.

  • Development: Announced in February 2024. Shot in New Zealand from August to October 2024 under the working title Backpack, with Jeff Cutter returning as cinematographer, on a $105 million budget. It is the first mainline Predator film rated PG-13.
  • No humans: Trachtenberg wanted no human co-lead, so he paired the Predator with a robot: "I know a company that makes robots" (Empire via JoBlo; EW via Reactor).
  • Yautja on screen: First film to say "Yautja" and "Yautja Prime." Britton Watkins built a subtitled Predator language. Dek is played by stuntman Dimitrius Schuster-Koloamatangi in a Studio Gillis suit with a mocap-enhanced face.
  • Influences: Frazetta, Malick, Conan the Barbarian, Mad Max 2, The Book of Eli and Shadow of the Colossus. The title's echo of Malick's 1973 Badlands is a WINK at most.
  • Weyland-Yutani (CANON): Synthetics Thia and Tessa, logo-stamped eyes (a gag borrowed from Alien: Romulus), MU/TH/UR voiced by Alison Wright, a base, ships, mercenaries, and a Tessa-piloted power loader echoing Aliens. The company is after the regenerating Kalisk for its weapons work.
  • Theories: Tessa's line about why Mother gave them feelings is CANON. "Mother runs the company" is FAN THEORY (/Film). Dek's mother as a matriarch tied to the Killer of Killers Warehouse is FAN THEORY (Looper). Yautja Prime as the KoK arena world is plausible but unconfirmed.
  • Timeline: Trachtenberg places it "well into the future" of both franchises, with Alien: Earth (2120) entirely before it. A 25th-century date is fan estimate. Alien Resurrection's Walmart buyout joke is the main continuity wrinkle.
  • Easter eggs: Per Trachtenberg to EW, there is a glimpse of Naru and an appearance by the Back Biter from KoK. The Duffer Brothers voice Kwei's ship computer. Cameron Brown went from the Alien: Earth xenomorph suit to a Badlands Drone Synth, a happy accident.
  • Blade Runner angle: No on-screen link. The hosts note a thematic echo between Tyrell's memories as emotional control and Tessa's question about feelings. Benjamin Wallfisch (Blade Runner 2049) co-scored with Sarah Schachner (Prey).
  • Box office and reception: $40.0M domestic opening, a franchise record, and $184.6M worldwide (The Numbers). A- CinemaScore, the franchise's best. 86% on Rotten Tomatoes (277 reviews), 71 on Metacritic. TheWrap raved, JoBlo found it tame, and The Guardian gave it two stars.
  • Crossover: Trachtenberg says it's not a stealth AvP but the link could "grow into a bigger thing." A third Trachtenberg Predator film and Schwarzenegger talks are reported.
  • Map update: Far future, Genna: Weyland-Yutani is CANON in the mainline Predator universe and still making synthetics centuries after Alien. The Yautja homeworld, language and clans are named. Dek, Thia and Bud become a clan, and a mother arrives.

item.title: The Weyland Files, Part 24: Alien: Earth (2025)
item.description:
The xenomorph comes to Earth. Pip and Alder dig into Noah Hawley's FX series, set in 2120: its long road through COVID and the 2023 strikes, the Bangkok shoot, the Peter Pan hybrids, five ruling corporations, the Maginot's specimens, Hawley's choice to leave out the Prometheus/Covenant origin story, the continuity knots, reviews and streaming numbers, and where Season 2 stands as of November 2026.

  • Development: First reported in 2019, announced at Disney's December 2020 Investor Day, and revealed as a pre-Alien prequel in 2022; FX says its scale exceeds Shogun's.
  • Production: Filming started in Thailand on July 19, 2023, stopped for the SAG-AFTRA strike, resumed April 2024 and wrapped mid-July 2024: 123 days, about 82 sets across 13 Bangkok studios.
  • World: In 2120, Weyland-Yutani, Lynch, Dynamic, Threshold and Prodigy run Earth and the colonized Solar System; Boy Kavalier's Prodigy builds hybrids, human minds in synthetic bodies.
  • Peter Pan: Wendy and the Lost Boys on Neverland; Hawley calls Peter "almost a sociopath" and children "bad liars" (Den of Geek).
  • The Maginot: A 65-year Weyland-Yutani specimen run with its own MU/TH/UR; the flashback episode "In Space, No One..."; new species including the Ocellus eye parasite.
  • Canon stance: Hawley built on the first two films and set aside the prequels' origin story (SXSW via Inverse; Empire via Popverse); per GamesRadar, Romulus and the show ran on "separate tracks."
  • Continuity knots: The Weyland-Yutani merger date, Nostromo-era tech on a ship launched around 2057, and why the Company in Aliens seems so ignorant (FAN THEORY fixes discussed).
  • Reception: RT 94%, Metacritic 85; FX's biggest streaming premiere (over 100M hours in 2025); four 2026 Emmy nominations; a Gotham award for Babou Ceesay.
  • Blade Runner bridge: Hybrids as replicant-like "children in adult bodies" and Kavalier as a Tyrell figure: labeled ANALYSIS, not canon.
  • Season 2 status: Renewed Nov 11, 2025; Peter Dinklage, Tracey Ullman, Sam Spruell and Jerome Flynn added; filming reported in London from summer 2026; no premiere date yet (2027 expected).
  • Map update: 2120 Earth ruled by five corporations; the Maginot (launched about 2057) crashes into New Siam; cyborgs, synthetics and hybrids; Ms. Yutani as CEO; Neverland seized by the hybrids; the xenomorph's origin marked as contested.

item.title: The Weyland Files, Part 23: Predator: Killer of Killers (2025)
item.description:
Pip and Alder open the Warehouse. Predator: Killer of Killers (2025) is Dan Trachtenberg and Joshua Wassung's secret animated feature from previs studio The Third Floor. It follows a Viking raider, a shinobi and a World War Two pilot who each kill a Predator and get collected for an alien arena. The hosts cover the Unreal Engine pipeline, the influences (Hard Boiled, Akira, Arcane, Frazetta, and yes, Best in Show), each chapter, the warlord's suspicious bone cape, the reception, and the timeline puzzle created by Naru, Dutch, Harrigan and the Raphael Adolini pistol.

  • Secret origin: Teased by 20th Century's Steve Asbell in October 2024, revealed and titled in April 2025, and released on Hulu June 6, 2025. It was one of three ideas Trachtenberg developed after Prey, alongside Badlands and one unmade story.
  • The Third Floor: The previs studio built an animation department from 2020. Per Cartoon Brew, it made the film in Unreal Engine with about 80% of compositing done in-engine, a team that peaked near 165, about 18 months of production, and a reported $50 million budget.
  • Look and influences: The team called the style "moving concept art," animated on twos, with Arcane talent involved. Influences include Hard Boiled, Jackie Chan, Akira, Frazetta and Conan, Spartan culture, Pulp Fiction over Twilight Zone: The Movie, and Christopher Guest's Best in Show.
  • The Shield / The Sword / The Bullet: Ursa in Karelia in 841, with a one-take shield-wall raid. The Kawakami brothers in Japan from 1609, both voiced by Louis Ozawa, Hanzo in Predators. Torres in 1942 under Vandy, voiced by Aliens' Michael Biehn.
  • The arena: On an unnamed Predator-ruled world, the Grendel King (voiced by Britton Watkins, later Badlands' language creator) wears a bone cape and a Yautja-skull mask. Xenomorph-tail bones are FAN THEORY; Trachtenberg says only that they "might" be other species.
  • The pistol: The Raphael Adolini flintlock is handed to Torres in the arena and left behind (CANON on screen). Where that falls relative to Harrigan's 1997 gift is open.
  • The Warehouse: Naru from Prey is in a stasis pod (CANON). The July 25, 2025 extended ending adds Dutch and Harrigan. Trachtenberg deliberately gave no year and says the Naru cameo sets up something after Badlands.
  • Yautja culture: Trachtenberg wants the Yautja as varied as humans (no "Wookiee" uniformity). The film shows warlords, arenas, atmospheric fighters and the collecting of worthy opponents.
  • Reception: 95% on Rotten Tomatoes (110 reviews) and 78 on Metacritic (18 critics). IndieWire's David Ehrlich called it artfully staged animated pulp; RogerEbert.com's Clint Worthington made the "Kool-Aid Man" complaint. It got three regional critics' nominations, and no viewership figures were found.
  • Shared universe: No Weyland-Yutani, xenomorph or Tyrell on screen. The real-world links are Michael Biehn and composer Benjamin Wallfisch, co-composer of Blade Runner 2049.
  • Map update: 841 Ursa; c.1629 Kenji; 1942 and after Torres. An undated arena on a Predator world, a vault of champions in stasis (Naru, Dutch, Harrigan), and the pistol in Yautja hands. The Yautja are now a collecting civilization.

item.title: The Weyland Files, Part 22: Alien: Romulus (2024)
item.description:
Back on the main line: Fede Alvarez's 2024 interquel, set in 2142 between Alien and Aliens. Pip and Alder cover the old Scott Free pitch revived after Disney bought Fox, the Hulu-to-theaters switch, the practical creature work, the Ian Holm "Rook" controversy and its home-video fix, the Prometheus black goo link, the box office and reviews, and the sequel's collapse after Ridley Scott took the franchise back in 2026.

  • Origins: Alvarez pitched an Alien film at Scott Free after Don't Breathe; Steve Asbell revived it after the Disney deal; it was first planned for Hulu, then moved to theaters.
  • Inspiration: The colony kids in the Aliens special edition, Alien: Isolation, Ron Cobb's concept art, and Dina from The Last of Us Part II (for Kay).
  • Production: Shot in story order in Budapest, March 9 to July 3, 2023; creatures by Legacy Effects, Studio Gillis and Weta Workshop; score by Benjamin Wallfisch, co-composer of Blade Runner 2049.
  • Rook: An Ash-model android with Ian Holm's likeness, used with his estate's permission; critics were split; Alvarez told Empire they "ran out of time" and leaned more on the puppet for the home release.
  • Andy: David Jonsson's synthetic "brother" and the film's Blade Runner-style question about whether implanted love counts.
  • Prometheus link: The xeno-derived Z-01 and the Engineer-like Offspring tie Romulus to Prometheus and Covenant (CANON on screen, plus CREATOR COMMENT); the Offspring also echoes Resurrection's Newborn.
  • Box office: $42M opening, $105.3M domestic, $350.9M worldwide (Box Office Mojo) on a reported $80M budget; $40M from IMAX.
  • Reception: RT 80%, Metacritic 64, CinemaScore B+; Gleiberman, Hoffman and Mottram were positive; LaSalle, Ehrlich and Ebiri were not; Oscar nomination for visual effects.
  • Aftermath: Alvarez finished a sequel script in 2025 but stepped back from directing; in August 2026 Scott called Romulus "okay" and said he is rewriting the next film; Film Stories (Oct 2026) reports Aaron Guzikowski is writing a Covenant-world Alien film.
  • Labels: CANON: the Nostromo cocoon, Rook as an Ash model, Z-01. WINK: the Isolation phones, the reused Aliens line, the pulse rifle precursor. FAN THEORY: the Company buried its xeno research before Aliens, and the xenomorph as humanity's cousin through the Engineers.
  • Map update: Feb 9, 2142, the cocoon is recovered from the Nostromo; Jackson's Star mining colony; the Renaissance station (Romulus and Remus) destroyed; Yvaga III; the Z-01 human-engineering program; Ash-model synthetics still in service.

item.title: The Weyland Files, Part 21: Prey (2022)
item.description:
Pip and Alder go back to 1719 and the northern Great Plains for Prey (2022), Dan Trachtenberg and Patrick Aison's Comanche-led Predator prequel. They cover how a side-story pitch rescued the franchise after The Predator (2018), the Comanche production and full-language dub, ADI's Feral Predator, Sarah Schachner's score, the streaming-record reception, and the Raphael Adolini pistol that links Naru to Mike Harrigan in 1997.

  • Development: Trachtenberg and Aison worked on the idea from 2016 and pitched it to producer John Davis while The Predator was in production, modeled on Rogue One and Solo. It was codenamed Skulls (December 2019) and titled Prey on November 12, 2021.
  • The Billy origin: As a third grader, Trachtenberg heard from older kids about a Billy versus Predator log-bridge duel that the 1987 film never shows. He calls Prey "spiritually" that movie.
  • Comanche production: Producer Jhane Myers (Comanche and Blackfeet) pushed for horses and period details. There were Native crew in every department, a pipe-ceremony blessing on Stoney Nakoda land, and the first full Comanche-language feature dub, performed by the original cast.
  • Production: Shot June to September 2021 near Calgary, Alberta. Jeff Cutter shot it anamorphic in natural light on a reported $65 million budget.
  • Feral Predator: Built by ADI, the shop behind the Alien 3, Resurrection and AVP xenomorphs, and played by 6'9" Dane DiLiegro. It has a skull mask, a bolt gun in place of the shoulder cannon, a Kratos-inspired shield and a red cloak shimmer. Trachtenberg calls it the slimmest Predator.
  • Music: Sarah Schachner was hired after Trachtenberg played Assassin's Creed Valhalla. Robert Mirabal contributed flute and vocals, and the score won a Hollywood Music in Media Award.
  • Reception: 94% on Rotten Tomatoes (291 reviews) and 71 on Metacritic, the franchise's best on both. Disney called it Hulu's most-watched premiere by hours (no figures released). It got six Emmy nominations and one win for sound editing, the franchise's first Emmy.
  • The pistol (CANON): The flintlock engraved "Raphael Adolini 1715" that the Elder gives Harrigan in Predator 2 belongs to Prey's French translator and ends up with Naru. This overwrites Dark Horse's 1996 Predator: 1718 pirate origin.
  • Labels: Billy Sole as Taabe reincarnated is an actor's reported reading (CREATOR COMMENT at most). How the pistol got back to the Yautja is FAN THEORY. The comic bear fights are a WINK at most. Prey's relationship to AVP's ancient Yautja history is unresolved.
  • Shared universe: There is no Weyland-Yutani, Tyrell or xenomorph on screen. The link runs through objects: Prey connects to Predator 2 by the pistol, and Predator 2 connects to Alien by the xenomorph skull.
  • Map update: 1719: the Feral is killed by Naru. A pistol dated 1715 passes from Adolini to Naru, then (unknown) back to the Yautja, then to Harrigan in 1997. The honor code is confirmed as at least three centuries old, and Yautja kit varies by hunter.

item.title: The Weyland Files, Part 20: Blade Runner: Black Lotus (2021)
item.description:
Pip and Alder cover Blade Runner: Black Lotus (2021-2022), the 13-episode CG anime from Alcon, Adult Swim and Sola Digital Arts. It is set in Los Angeles in 2032, during the replicant ban, and follows Elle, an amnesiac replicant. Topics: the creative team, the look and the music, the Doll Hunt, the Wallace family drama that explains why Niander Wallace is blind, an Easter egg catalog, the mixed reviews, and the series being written off in 2022.

  • Placement: Set in October 2032, ten years after Black Out 2022 and four years before Nexus Dawn. Producer Andrew Kosove told SYFY Wire it sits "about halfway" between the two films (CANON).
  • Team: Co-directed by Kenji Kamiyama and Shinji Aramaki. Shinichiro Watanabe was creative producer and Joseph Chou executive producer. Eugene Son wrote the first and last episodes.
  • Cast: Jessica Henwick (Elle), Will Yun Lee (Joseph), Samira Wiley (Davis), Wes Bentley (Wallace Jr.) and Brian Cox (Wallace Sr.). Barkhad Abdi returns as a younger Doc Badger.
  • Look and sound: Chou wanted a style that was neither cartoonish nor photoreal, and lighting was the priority. Critics split over the "waxy" faces. Michael Hodges and Gerald Trottman wrote a Vangelis-style score.
  • The Doll Hunt: A senator and police chief hunt replicants for sport, a riff on The Most Dangerous Game that it shares with Predator. The Predator link is thematic only, and anything more is FAN THEORY.
  • Wallace's eyes: Wallace Jr. uses Elle to kill his father, a reversal of Roy killing Tyrell. Elle then blinds him in the former Tyrell building, which explains the blind Wallace in Nexus Dawn and 2049 (CANON).
  • Easter eggs: The Bradbury Building, the Esper machine, a Voight-Kampff test, Nexus-8 serial numbers in the eye, Spinners, neon umbrellas and a finale called "Time to Die". All CANON details, staged as WINKS.
  • Comics crossover: Marlowe first appeared in Titan's Blade Runner 2029 comic. The Black Lotus comics Leaving L.A. (2022) and Las Vegas (2025) continue Elle's story.
  • Joseph: A former Blade Runner haunted by the replicant singer Selene. The idea that he is a replicant is FAN THEORY.
  • Reception: 71% on Rotten Tomatoes from 7 reviews, and a Metascore of 61 from 4 critics. GameSpot called it a stylish "replica", and Anime News Network compared it to a chain-restaurant combo meal.
  • Business: Warner Bros. Discovery wrote the series off in September 2022, seven months after the finale.
  • Map update: In 2032 the ban is being broken in secret. Wallace Sr. dies, Wallace Jr. is blinded, and Joseph dies destroying the replicant labs. There are no new Alien or Predator pins, but the theme of makers killed by what they made grows stronger.

item.title: The Weyland Files, Part 19: Raised by Wolves
item.description:
Pip and Alder land on Kepler-22b for Raised by Wolves (HBO Max, 2020-2022), Aaron Guzikowski's spec-born series. Ridley Scott directed the first two episodes, and the show is shot by Prometheus's cinematographer and co-scored by Prometheus's composer. Both creators say it is not in the Alien universe. Then, in October 2026, its creator was hired to write a new Alien film.

  • Origins: Guzikowski (Prisoners) wrote the pilot on spec. It grew from his being a father and from Ash in Alien, which got him thinking about androids made of flesh. Ridley storyboarded the whole pilot.
  • Business: TNT ordered it straight to series on October 8, 2018; it moved to HBO Max on October 29, 2019 with executive Sarah Aubrey; premiered September 3, 2020; renewed September 17, 2020.
  • Production: Shot in the Western Cape, South Africa, from January 2019; the settlement set was built at Lourensford Wine Estate; Chris Seagers was production designer; Ridley planned it with his "Ridleygrams."
  • Crew pins: Ridley Scott directed eps 1-2 (his TV directing debut); Luke Scott directed eps 3, 4 and 10; DP Dariusz Wolski (Prometheus, Covenant); music by Ben Frost and Marc Streitenfeld (Prometheus).
  • Androids: Amanda Collin's Mother, a reprogrammed Mithraic necromancer whose look Ridley designed, and Abubakar Salim's Father. Their white fluid is A.V. Club's "milk" thread going back to Ash.
  • Themes: Atheists vs. the Sol-worshipping Mithraic; an android giving birth to a serpent; devolved earlier humans; parallels to Prometheus's Engineers and David (Screen Rant).
  • Reception: Season 1: RT 74%, Metacritic 64. Season 2: RT 86%, Metacritic 84. WSJ called Mother the most memorable female space entity since Ripley.
  • Cancellation: Announced June 3, 2022 by Salim after the Warner Bros. Discovery merger; pulled from HBO Max in December 2022; moved to Roku/Tubi FAST channels in 2023.
  • Creator verdicts (CREATOR COMMENT): Guzikowski called it a "close cousin" that doesn't necessarily link up. Ridley's Reddit AMA answer was "Interesting question but, no," and he added that Alien feels like it comes some time before Wolves.
  • Fan theories: Secret Prometheus prequel; necromancer makers are Engineers; Mother named after MU/TH/UR. All FAN THEORY. No confirmed W-Y or Tyrell Easter eggs were found.
  • October 2026 news: Per THR (via A.V. Club, Nerdist, Syfy Wire), Guzikowski is writing a new Alien film developed by Ridley Scott that continues the Prometheus/Covenant line. It is not a Romulus sequel, and Scott is not attached to direct.
  • Map update: Creators say no. Gray pin for the "after Alien" aside. Crew pins (Wolski, Streitenfeld, the Scotts). Theme pins (synthetic body with a replicant's question, android pregnancy echoing 2049, Engineer-like makers). A people arrow from Wolves into the next Alien film.
  • Unverified: Exact in-world year (about 150 years ahead, per Guzikowski), viewership, season 3 plans, and details of the new Alien film.

item.title: The Weyland Files, Part 18: Underwater (2020)
item.description:
Pip and Alder dive seven miles down with Underwater (2020), William Eubank's deep-sea creature feature written by Brian Duffield and Adam Cozad: a Chernin/Fox production shot in New Orleans in 2017, held in limbo by the Disney-Fox merger, released as the last film under the Twentieth Century Fox name, and later revealed to end with Cthulhu. Then they put its one tie to the Scott-verse, a Weyland-Yutani logo on Captain Lucien's kit, on trial.

  • Development: Story by Brian Duffield, screenplay with Adam Cozad's revisions; produced by Peter Chernin, Jenno Topping and Tonia Davis; financed by TSG and Chernin with Fox/Disney distributing.
  • Director: William Eubank, ex-Panavision camera tech, director of Love (2011) and The Signal (2014); cinematography by Bojan Bazelli.
  • Production: Shot in New Orleans in 2017 using dry-for-wet, tanks and VFX; pressure suits built with Legacy Effects (Stan Winston Studio lineage), some topping 200 lb; about a year of post-production.
  • Release: January 10, 2020, after the Disney-Fox merger delay; the last release under the Twentieth Century Fox name before the January 17, 2020 rebrand.
  • Box office and reception: About $7M opening; roughly $17.3M domestic and $39-41M worldwide on a $50-65M budget; RT 49%, Metacritic 48, CinemaScore C; one VES nomination for compositing.
  • The monster (CREATOR COMMENT): The script's whale-like "Behemoth" turned into Cthulhu during design; Eubank called the film a "secret Lovecraft love story."
  • The strap (WINK): Eubank posted on Alien Day (April 26, 2020) about a Weyland-Yutani logo on Lucien's equipment. He confirmed the egg exists, but nothing gives it any continuity weight.
  • Tian Industries as a W-Y front (FAN THEORY): Speculation only. A W-Y logo around 2050 also clashes with Prometheus's stand-alone Weyland Corp in 2093.
  • Influences: The Abyss (Eubank is a fan), Aliens (T.J. Miller: "The Abyss meets Aliens"), the 1989 undersea cycle (Eubank says he hadn't seen Leviathan or DeepStar Six), Alien, and Prometheus-style marketing.
  • Lovecraft lineage: Giger's Necronomicon, Dan O'Bannon, Prometheus vs. del Toro's At the Mountains of Madness. This is a family tree of influence, not a shared timeline.
  • Score and sound: Marco Beltrami and Brandon Roberts; the groaning hull and helmet breathing work like the Nostromo's sound design.
  • Map update: Lovecraft influence pin; W-Y strap goes in the Easter egg drawer (WINK); Tian joins the corporate-dystopia lineage (theme); Fox/Legacy craft pin. Verdict: a relative, not a resident.
  • Unverified: On-screen year (2050 per plot summaries), which ending Eubank preferred, and the exact shot showing the logo.

item.title: The Weyland Files, Part 17: The Predator (2018)
item.description:
Pip and Alder take on Shane Black's The Predator (2018): the director who played Hawkins in 1987 returns with co-writer Fred Dekker, a Halloween-set, Amblin-flavored sequel with a misfit ensemble, a heavily reshot third act, two filmed-then-cut endings featuring Ripley and Newt, a pre-release casting controversy, and the most explicit nod to Alien vs. Predator in any main-line Predator film.

  • Hawkins returns: Shane Black, the first man killed on screen in Predator (1987), was announced as director and co-writer with Fred Dekker in June 2014; John Davis produced, as on every Predator film.
  • The pitch: Black wanted to "event-ise" the Predator with a Close Encounters sense of wonder; Fox's Stacey Snider praised that it "didn't read like a Predator film."
  • Timeline: Black said it is a sequel, set between Predator 2 and Predators, and that Predators is canon but has not happened yet (CREATOR COMMENT).
  • Reshoots: About three quarters of the final act was rewritten; the daytime ending with friendly "Emissary" Predators and hybrids was cut; Black's proposed "Predator A.M./P.M." release was declined.
  • Ghost endings: Breanna Watkins filmed alternate endings as Ripley and an adult Newt emerging from a pod, with a backstory involving time travel and cloning; both were replaced by the Predator Killer armor. Not canon.
  • Ms. Yutani: Françoise Yip's lines were cut and she was credited as "Tracking Supervisor"; whether she was playing Ms. Yutani is reported, not confirmed on screen.
  • Controversy: Olivia Munn had a scene with registered sex offender Steven Wilder Striegel removed days before release; Black apologized after first defending the casting.
  • Box office: $24.6M opening, $51.0M domestic, $160.5M worldwide on an $88M budget (Box Office Mojo); a 65% second-weekend drop.
  • Reception: Rotten Tomatoes 34%, Metacritic 48, CinemaScore C+; praise for the ensemble and Sterling K. Brown, criticism of the climax and of the film's treatment of autism.
  • Easter eggs: Jake Busey as Sean Keyes, son of Predator 2's Peter Keyes; surveillance photos from 1987 and 1997; Lex's Xenomorph-tail spear and the Predator 2 spear in Stargazer's trophy case (reportedly added in reshoots); a school named for producer Lawrence Gordon.
  • Fan theory: Predator 2's task force, Requiem's Colonel Stevens and Stargazer form one continuous secret government Predator program.
  • Map update: Around 2018, Stargazer studies Predators; Predators genetically upgrade themselves; a defector delivers the Predator Killer armor; humanity's stockpile of Predator technology keeps growing.

item.title: The Weyland Files, Part 16: The 2049 Shorts
item.description:
Pip and Alder go through the three official prequel shorts that fill the thirty-year gap before Blade Runner 2049: Shinichirō Watanabe's anime Blade Runner Black Out 2022 and Luke Scott's 2036: Nexus Dawn and 2048: Nowhere to Run. They cover who made them and why, what each adds to the timeline, where the dates don't line up, and whether the Blackout of 2022 clears the way for Peter Weyland's androids.

  • Origins: Villeneuve asked three filmmakers for prequel shorts; produced by Alcon with Scott Free (live action) and CygamesPictures (anime); Warner Bros. in North America, Sony internationally.
  • Luke Scott: Ridley's son (director of Morgan, 2016) got the job through 3AM, the company behind the Alien: Covenant shorts; scripts by Hampton Fancher and Michael Green; production designer Paul Inglis, DoP Pierre Gill.
  • 2036: Nexus Dawn: released August 30, 2017; Jared Leto's Wallace asks lawmakers (including Benedict Wong) to lift the prohibition, calls the stars "our only hope", and has a Nexus-9 cut its own throat to prove obedience. Shot in Budapest.
  • 2048: Nowhere to Run: released mid-September 2017; Dave Bautista's Sapper Morton protects a mother and daughter, reveals his strength and drops his papers, which leads the LAPD to his farm. Shot in a disused limestone mine; Adam Savage cameo.
  • Blade Runner Black Out 2022: fifteen-minute anime premiered on Crunchyroll in late September 2017; Watanabe called Blade Runner his greatest influence; Shukou Murase designs; Flying Lotus score; replicants Iggy and Trixie and human technician Ren set off an EMP that wipes Tyrell's records.
  • Analysis: rebels, refugee, creator; Iggy and Trixie as a remix of Roy and Pris; eyes as identity; Wallace's products as "a pitch deck that bleeds".
  • Canon status: all three CANON (rights holder, feature writers, Villeneuve sign-off); dates for the ban (2023 per a timeline reported by Dazed) and Wallace's takeover (2028 per the Blade Runner wiki) are a bit fuzzy.
  • Alien links: shared Luke Scott/Scott Free/3AM short-film pipeline (human link); Wallace's colonization pitch alongside Weyland-Yutani's "Building Better Worlds" (thematic); corporate soldier obsession (thematic); no WINKS or CANON found.
  • Alder's fan theory: the 2022 Blackout wipes out Tyrell's biological line a year before Peter Weyland's 2023 TED talk pitches mechanical androids. FAN THEORY; he puts the odds the date match was intentional at five to ten percent.
  • Watch order: the hosts argue release order vs story order vs feature-first and settle on Black Out, then the feature, then the Luke Scott shorts.
  • Map update: 2022 Blackout and data wipe; replicant-on-replicant off-world war; 2023 ban and Tyrell bankruptcy; Wallace buys Tyrell; 2036 Nexus-9 pitch; 2048 Sapper exposed; Alder's score goes to four and a half out of ten.

item.title: The Weyland Files, Part 15: Blade Runner 2049 (2017)
item.description:
Pip and Alder take on Denis Villeneuve's Blade Runner 2049 (2017): the thirty-five-year road from Alcon's rights deal to a Budapest shoot, Roger Deakins' Oscar, a late score swap, a box office disappointment that critics loved, the replicant miracle, the still-open Deckard question, and whether a Sulaco-shaped ship and Engineer-like bodies move Alder's Alien score at all.

  • Development: Alcon's Andrew Kosove and Broderick Johnson bought rights from Bud Yorkin; Ridley Scott announced to direct in August 2011, then chose Alien: Covenant and stayed as executive producer; Hampton Fancher and Michael Green wrote.
  • Director and cast: Villeneuve (via Prisoners) hesitated over the legacy; Ford approached in 2014; Gosling, de Armas, Hoeks, Wright, Davis, Juri, Bautista, Leto (after Bowie was considered), Olmos returns as Gaff.
  • Production: July to November 2016 at Korda and Origo Studios near Budapest; Budapest Stock Exchange as Las Vegas; Inota and Kelenföld power plants; a subcontractor killed during set strike.
  • Craft: Deakins' single-camera approach and first Oscar on his fourteenth nomination; Dennis Gassner's physical sets; Zimmer and Wallfisch replaced Jóhann Jóhannsson in July 2017 and reworked Vangelis' "Tears in Rain".
  • Box office: $150-185M budget; domestic opening about $31.5M (Deadline) or $32.75M (Box Office Mojo) against $43-47M projections; $259M original worldwide, about $278M lifetime; THR estimated Alcon losses up to $80M; Scott: "Slow. Long. Too long."
  • Reception: 88% Rotten Tomatoes, 81 Metacritic, A- CinemaScore; praise from Bradshaw, Turan, A.O. Scott; criticism of its women from Helen Lewis, Charlotte Gush, Anna Smith; Rutger Hauer critical; five Oscar nominations, two wins.
  • Themes: replicant birth as the "miracle", memory and identity, Joi as a product one level below K, the wasp/bee empathy callback, environmental collapse, two replicants saving Deckard in rain and snow.
  • Deckard question: Scott says replicant (CREATOR COMMENT), Fancher says "absolutely not", Green wants it open; Wallace raises it on screen; still unresolved.
  • Easter eggs: origami sheep, Atari/Pan Am/Coca-Cola survivals, Sony jukebox, Pale Fire baseline test, the novel's goat, Deckard's rebuilt blaster, Rachael's N7 serial, the opening farm scene adapted from a cut 1982 script idea (WINKS).
  • Alien links: Sulaco-like ship likely Syd Mead's handwriting (WINK); Engineer-like replicant bodies (design echo, FAN THEORY); Wallace as a Weyland analog (FAN THEORY); Scott calling Ash "the first replication of a human" (CREATOR COMMENT, thematic only). No new CANON.
  • Fan theories with director answers: Villeneuve to Fandom on Mark Millar's implant theory, Luv, Ana's illness (agreed it's a ruse) and K being "obviously a replicant".
  • Map update: Nexus-8 open lifespans (2020); Blackout and prohibition (around 2022); Wallace buys Tyrell and launches the obedient Nexus-9; Ana Stelline born June 10, 2021; 2049 Los Angeles behind a sea wall; Tyrell's two heirs, Wallace by purchase and Weyland by argument (FAN THEORY on a WINK).

item.title: The Weyland Files, Part 14: Alien: Covenant (2017)
item.description:
Pip and Alder close out the prequels with Ridley Scott's Alien: Covenant (2017) and its prologue shorts, The Crossing, The Last Supper, Meet Walter and Advent, plus the In Utero VR teaser. David builds the perfect organism, Weyland-Yutani is back, and Ridley Scott says he should have made Blade Runner 2 instead.

  • Development: Lindelof steps away; drafts by Jack Paglen, Michael Green, Dante Harper and John Logan; the Alien: Paradise Lost working title; xenomorphs restored after Prometheus feedback.
  • Prologue shorts: The Crossing (Shaw rebuilds David; the Engineer city is bombed), Luke Scott's The Last Supper and Meet Walter ("Created to serve"), Advent on the Blu-ray, and David Karlak's In Utero VR teaser.
  • Production: Australian incentives, Milford Sound, Wolski and Scalia, Creature NFX and Odd Studios, organic creature design drawn from La Specola's wax anatomy and San Diego Zoo advice.
  • Creatures: Neomorphs, the first back-burster, the protomorph, the Pompeii-like necropolis and David's lab.
  • David and Walter: Fassbender times two, the flute scene, the Judas kiss, Michelangelo, Wagner's Entry of the Gods into Valhalla, and the Ozymandias misattribution.
  • Themes: Creation without love, broken covenants, Paradise Lost and Frankenstein, Oram's faith and the xenomorph that mimics its father.
  • Box office and reception: $36.2M #1 opening, a 71% second-weekend drop, about $240.9M worldwide on a $97M budget (Box Office Mojo); 65% on Rotten Tomatoes, 65 on Metacritic, CinemaScore B.
  • Blade Runner watch: Michael Green's credits on both Covenant and 2049; Scott telling Empire (2023) he should have done Blade Runner 2; his 2024 THR regret about not controlling both franchises (CREATOR COMMENT, not continuity).
  • Theories: David as father of the xenomorph versus the ancient derelict's eggs; whether the Engineer world was their only world; Shaw's death; David as Milton's Satan.
  • The sequel saga: From a planned trilogy to cancellation reports to Scott's August 2026 statements about a David-centered third prequel (not confirmed for production).
  • Map update: 2093 The Crossing; 2104 the Weyland-Yutani colony ship Covenant (2,000 colonists, 1,140 embryos) bound for Origae-6; the Weyland/Yutani merger complete; Walter line; neomorphs; David in control of the Covenant with xenomorph embryos, 18 years before the Nostromo.

item.title: The Weyland Files, Part 13: Prometheus (2012)
item.description:
Pip and Alder go back to the founding myth: Ridley Scott's Prometheus (2012), plus its three viral shorts, Peter Weyland's TED 2023 talk, Happy Birthday, David and Quiet Eye. Engineers, black goo, a billionaire who wants to be a god, and the first official Alien product to wink at Tyrell.

  • Development: The abandoned Scott and Cameron sequel, Fox's 2009 "reboot", Jon Spaihts' Christmas Day 2009 draft, Damon Lindelof's rewrite, and the title change from Paradise to Prometheus.
  • Alien: Engineers: What Spaihts' leaked draft had (xenomorphs, an underwater star map, Shaw as "Watts", the derelict as the same ship) and what changed.
  • The shoot: 82 days across Pinewood's 007 Stage, Shepperton, Iceland's Hekla and Dettifoss, Wadi Rum and Skye; native 3D from Dariusz Wolski; fewer than six green screens.
  • Design: Arthur Max, Giger's 11 months of murals, Neville Page's Greco-Roman Engineers, the Deacon, the Joseph Wright orrery, and the Steve Jobs glass helmets.
  • Performances: Fassbender's David (built from Blade Runner's replicants, HAL, Bowie and O'Toole), Rapace, Theron, Elba and Guy Pearce under old-age makeup.
  • Viral shorts: Luke Scott's TED 2023 ("we are the gods now"), Johnny Hardstaff's David 8 ad and Quiet Eye with its Yutani logo and LV-426 signal note.
  • Themes: Creators and defiance, Paradise Lost, von Daniken, faith versus science, the self-surgery, fathers and synthetic sons, and Scott's crucified-Engineer idea (CREATOR COMMENT).
  • Box office and reception: $403.4M worldwide on a $130M budget (Box Office Mojo); roughly 73-74% on Rotten Tomatoes, 64 on Metacritic, CinemaScore B; Ebert's four stars against Bradshaw, Chang and Empire's doubts.
  • Blade Runner watch: Lindelof and Fassbender cite Blade Runner (CREATOR COMMENT); the Weyland note on the Blu-ray referencing Tyrell, which producer Charles de Lauzirika calls an in-joke (WINK).
  • Predator links: Ian Whyte (the Scar Predator) as an Engineer, and Dark Horse's Fire and Stone crossover (comic tie-in).
  • Theories: Black goo as xenomorph origin, Vickers the android, the Engineer as the Alien Space Jockey (mostly debunked), and when Weyland and Yutani merge (FAN THEORY).
  • Map update: 2089 star map on Skye; 2093 arrival at LV-223 (not LV-426); Weyland born 1990, Weyland Corp founded 2012, David unveiled 2024, Yutani loses a patent suit in 2029 (viral timeline); Weyland dies 2093; the Engineers and the Deacon arrive on the map.

item.title: The Weyland Files, Part 12: Predators (2010)
item.description:
Pip and Alder parachute onto a Predator game preserve with Predators (2010), Robert Rodriguez's long-shelved 1990s script, reworked by Alex Litvak and Michael Finch and directed by Nimród Antal. They cover the film's deliberate break from the AVP films, its Aliens-style title and strategy, a cast that looks remarkable in hindsight, the Hawaii and Texas shoot, the Super Predator vs. classic Predator feud, the returning 1987 creature design, the reviews and box office, and the Xenomorph skull that got in anyway. Plus Litvak's unmade sequel, which would have ended with Colonial Marines.

  • Script history: Rodriguez wrote it in the mid-1990s around Desperado (1994 or 1995 depending on the source). Fox passed on cost (about $150M per AvP Galaxy) and on technology. In 2009 Fox executive Alex Young revived it, and Rodriguez produced through Troublemaker Studios.
  • The old script (reported): per Looper's description of an unconfirmed circulating copy, it featured Dutch, a Spanish galleon and a prison or gladiator planet, plus a role reportedly written for Van Damme.
  • Director and title: Rodriguez picked Antal on the strength of Armored. Rodriguez said the title nods to Aliens and that he wanted the Cameron approach of making a new film rather than a copy (CREATOR COMMENT).
  • Cast: Adrien Brody (who put on 25 lb of muscle), Topher Grace, Alice Braga, Walton Goggins, Oleg Taktarov, Mahershala Ali, Danny Trejo, Louis Ozawa Changchien, and Laurence Fishburne, who reportedly shot for two days.
  • Production: $40M budget and a 53-day shoot from September 28, 2009, including 22 days at Kolekole, Hawaii. About 60% was shot in Texas (Austin, Canyon Lake Gorge, Hamilton Pool).
  • Creatures: KNB EFX's Berger and Nicotero, both Winston alumni, built the suits. Derek Mears plays the classic Predator, and Brian Steele and Carey Jones play the Berserker, Falconer and Tracker. A creature reportedly based on the abandoned 1987 Boss Film design appears.
  • The preserve: an unnamed planet holding many prey species, which finally realizes the Thomas brothers' original multi-species idea. The premise echoes the novel Predator: Forever Midnight.
  • Score: John Debney (Silvestri was unavailable because of The A-Team) wrote a Silvestri-style score with Tibetan long horns. "Long Tall Sally" plays over the credits.
  • Box office and reviews: $24.8M opening (third place) and $127.2M worldwide (Box Office Mojo). 65% on Rotten Tomatoes, 51 on Metacritic, C+ CinemaScore. Reviews from A.O. Scott, Michael Phillips, Ebert, Nashawaty, Gingold (Fangoria) and NPR.
  • Easter eggs: a Xenomorph skull at the camp (CANON WINK), a body with chestburster-style ribs, a line echoing Hicks in Aliens, Hanzo's name, the "ugly" line in Russian, the mud, and the minigun. A Fox logo in heat vision and Dutch/Harrigan cameos were both dropped.
  • Theories: AVP is ignored but never contradicted (CANON-compatible, with separation as a CREATOR COMMENT). Litvak's "Die Hard on a Predator ship" sequel ending with Colonial Marines (CREATOR COMMENT, unmade). The preserve and the Killer of Killers stasis vault as one system (FAN THEORY). Predator 2's alien skulls coming from preserves like this one (FAN THEORY).
  • Unverified: the exact year of the script and its contents, whether the Edwin ambush creature is the 1987 Boss design itself, what the commentary meant about the Berserker's "jaw from an Alien film," and the film's on-screen year.
  • Map update: Isabelle's dialogue puts the first film in Guatemala in 1987, on screen. New pins: a Predator game preserve planet with many species, interstellar abduction technology, two Predator tribes in a blood feud, hunting beasts and drones, Noland's decade on the planet, and a second Xenomorph skull confirming that Predators hunt Aliens.

item.title: The Weyland Files, Part 11: Aliens vs. Predator: Requiem (2007)
item.description:
Pip and Alder head to Gunnison, Colorado, for Aliens vs. Predator: Requiem (2007): the Brothers Strause and their effects house Hydraulx, a leaner R-rated sequel shot in Vancouver, the Predalien and the "cleaner" Predator called Wolf, the infamous darkness, a bruising critical reception, and the two-minute coda that hands Predator technology to a Ms. Yutani.

  • Fast sequel: The Strause brothers were hired in late spring 2006; shooting began September 23, 2006 in Vancouver on a 52-day schedule, on a $40M budget.
  • Paper trail: Produced by John Davis with Alien's Brandywine producers David Giler and Walter Hill; Shane Salerno's earlier Afghanistan draft became the comic Sand Trap.
  • Near-miss cameo: The directors wanted Adam Baldwin back as Predator 2's Agent Garber; Robert Joy played the new Colonel Stevens instead.
  • Creatures: ADI's Predalien (Predator skull under the dome, yellow pigment for visibility) and Wolf, nicknamed for Harvey Keitel's cleaner in Pulp Fiction; Hydraulx did about 460 of 500 effects shots.
  • The darkness: Colin Strause said the rain and blackout hid "guys in suits"; a 2016 behind-the-scenes clip showed DP Daniel Pearl saying it was not bright enough.
  • Sound: Brian Tyler's score blends Aliens and Alien 3 textures with Predator's bongos; the original Aliens creature sounds were remastered.
  • Box office: About $41.8M domestic and roughly $129M-$130M worldwide (sources differ) against $40M.
  • Reception: Rotten Tomatoes 12%, Metacritic 29, CinemaScore C; two Razzie nominations; Entertainment Weekly and the New York Times were kinder.
  • The Yutani coda: Colonel Stevens gives Wolf's plasma pistol to Ms. Yutani (CANON); Greg Strause told io9 a third film would have tied that gun to humanity's space tech and led into Alien (CREATOR COMMENT).
  • Canon: A direct sequel to AVP; the Gunnison nuke is never mentioned again; a secret government Predator program linking Predator 2, Requiem and The Predator is FAN THEORY built from canon pieces.
  • Map update: 2004: the Predalien lands in Gunnison; first look at the Predator homeworld; the town is nuked; Predator tech passes to Yutani, completing the AVP "corporate origin duology."

item.title: The Weyland Files, Part 10: Alien vs. Predator (2004)
item.description:
Pip and Alder dig into Alien vs. Predator (2004): thirteen years of development hell from the Dark Horse comics and Peter Briggs's 1991 spec, Paul W.S. Anderson's ancient-astronaut pyramid under the Antarctic ice, the practical creature work shot in Prague, a rough critical reception against a very profitable box office run, and the biggest continuity headache in the series so far: Charles Bishop Weyland.

  • Development: The crossover began in Dark Horse Presents #34-36 (1989-90); Peter Briggs wrote a spec in 1991 that producer Lawrence Gordon bought the same day; Fox did not move until 2002.
  • Weaver vs. Briggs: Sigourney Weaver (2015) said she asked for Ripley to die because Fox was heading toward AVP; Briggs disputes the timeline. Both labeled CREATOR COMMENT.
  • Anderson's pitch: An eight-year-old story adapting the Machiko Noguchi comics; producer John Davis wanted Earth, and Anderson chose remote Bouvet Island to avoid contradicting Alien.
  • Inspirations: Erich von Daniken, Lovecraft's At the Mountains of Madness, Aztec/Egyptian/Cambodian art, Hell in the Pacific, the Predator 2 ship interior, and Ron Cobb's unused Alien pyramid art.
  • Production: Barrandov Studios, Prague; sets for about $2M vs. an estimated $20M in LA; ADI's Gillis and Woodruff; a 4.8 m practical Queen run by 12 puppeteers; about 70% practical shots.
  • Box office: $38.3M opening, $80.3M domestic, $177.4M worldwide on a roughly $60M budget (Box Office Mojo).
  • Reception: Rotten Tomatoes about 22%, Metacritic 29, CinemaScore B; the PG-13 rating and dark fight lighting drew fire.
  • Charles Bishop Weyland: The role was written for Lance Henriksen; Anderson says the Bishop androids were modeled on the founder's face (CREATOR COMMENT).
  • Peter vs. Charles: Prometheus's Peter Weyland conflicts; the two being related is FAN THEORY; Lindelof flagging the clash to Scott is reported CREATOR COMMENT.
  • Easter eggs: The Piper Maru (X-Files nod), a mercenary named Mark Verheiden (Dark Horse writer), Nostromo-style color-coded crew, Lex's spear later seen in The Predator (2018).
  • Canon status: Comfortable in Predator continuity, contested in Alien continuity; Disney reportedly treats Alien, Predator and AVP as separate licenses.
  • Map update: Ancient Predator visits; a 100-year hunt cycle (1904, 2004); Weyland Industries in 2004 doing satellites and robotics; the Predalien born aboard the Predator ship.

item.title: The Weyland Files, Part 9: Soldier (1998)
item.description:
Pip and Alder dig into Soldier (1998), Paul W. S. Anderson's film of David Webb Peoples' 1984 script, starring Kurt Russell as Sergeant Todd 3465. Some people call it a Blade Runner "sidequel." We go through where the script came from, the production chaos, the design work by a Blade Runner veteran and every Easter egg on Todd's service record, then rule on whether any of it counts as canon.

  • Origins: Peoples says he wrote Soldier quickly in 1984 after seeing The Terminator, and that he never meant it to tie in with Blade Runner (interview for Danny Stewart's book Soldier: From Script to Screen). In 1998 he told Cinescape that, to him, the two films share a universe.
  • Event Horizon link: Russell trained for 18 months before filming, which delayed Soldier. Anderson used the gap to make Event Horizon.
  • The cabbage: Russell broke his left ankle about a week into the shoot. Anderson later admitted, on the AVP DVD commentary of all places, that he tripped over an ornamental cabbage. The crew filmed his scenes lying down first, then sitting, then standing.
  • Design: Production designer David L. Snyder, the art director on Blade Runner, called Soldier a companion piece.
  • Spinner: A Blade Runner Spinner sits in the junk on Arcadia 234 (WINK).
  • Service record: Todd's listed campaigns include the Tannhauser Gate and the Shoulder of Orion, next to battles from Star Trek II and medals named after Kurt Russell's other films (WINK).
  • Aliens guns: Todd's weapons record lists the USCM Smartgun and the M41A pulse rifle. It's a WINK, but it's the first frame in this series where Aliens and Blade Runner share the screen.
  • Event Horizon debris: A piece of the Lewis and Clark shows up in the garbage in 2036, eleven years before that ship's 2047 mission. That's a WINK, plus a timeline puzzle.
  • Box office and reviews: It cost $60M and made $14.6M in the US (Box Office Mojo). Rotten Tomatoes has it at 19%, and its CinemaScore was B+.
  • Legacy: Anderson wishes he had told Todd's backstory in flashback. Peoples has never watched the film. Arrow Video released it on 4K in 2026.
  • Verdict: Soldier is not CANON for the Blade Runner franchise. Several creators have tied the two together (CREATOR COMMENT), but Peoples later disputed the link. Todd fighting alongside Roy, and Mekum's program filling a gap left by a replicant ban, are FAN THEORY.
  • Map update: 1996, the soldier program starts. 2016 to 2019, the off-world battles. 2036, Todd is dumped on Arcadia 234, the same year as Nexus Dawn (a coincidence, FAN THEORY). Arcadia works as the shared universe's junk drawer.

item.title: The Weyland Files, Part 8: Event Horizon (1997)
item.description:
Our first edge case: Paul W. S. Anderson's 1997 "haunted house in space." Pip and Alder trace Philip Eisner's script, the Notre Dame cathedral ship, the brutal four-week post-production forced by Titanic's delay, the lost footage, the box office flop and the cult rebirth, then test every claimed link to Alien and the wider Scott-verse. Dedicated to Sam Neill (1947-2026).

  • Origins: Eisner pitched a haunted house in space inspired by The Shining; Predator producer Lawrence Gordon and Lloyd Levin developed it at Golar Productions; Paramount greenlit it about ten weeks before shooting.
  • Anderson's choice: Anderson picked Event Horizon after Kurt Russell postponed Soldier; Andrew Kevin Walker did uncredited hell-and-damnation rewrites.
  • Influences: Lovecraft, The Haunting, 2001, Alien, Warhammer 40,000, Hawking, Solaris, Hellraiser, Bosch and Bruegel, the Mary Celeste.
  • Design: A "techno-medieval" cruciform ship built from Notre Dame scans; a Lament Configuration-inspired gravity drive; about 28 miniatures.
  • The Alien lineage: Cinematographer Adrian Biddle was a focus puller on Alien and the cinematographer of Aliens.
  • Post-production: Titanic's delay cut the edit to about four weeks; test screenings went badly; about 130 minutes became 96; the extra footage was reportedly lost (Anderson's salt-mine story).
  • Score: Michael Kamen with Orbital; The Prodigy over the end credits; the "libera te tutemet ex inferis" signal.
  • Reception: $9.5M opening and $26.7M domestic (Box Office Mojo); CinemaScore D+; RT 36%; Metacritic 35; Ebert's "foreboding and afterboding."
  • Cult afterlife: Home video success, a 4K release in 2021, Variety's top 100 horror list in 2024, influence on Dead Space and Sunshine, IDW's Dark Descent and Inferno comics; the Amazon/Wingard series is still unconfirmed.
  • Labels: No CANON link to Alien, Predator or Blade Runner. CREATOR COMMENT: Alien influenced the film and the ship. WINK: the tagline and the derelict-like chamber. FAN THEORY: a Warhammer prequel, or an Alien-universe prequel built on the gravity drive.
  • Map update: A dotted-line pin at 2047 near Neptune (the launch was in 2040); a United States Aerospace Command government space program instead of a corporation; artificial black hole FTL; the creative bridge through Gordon, Biddle and Anderson (Soldier, AVP).

item.title: The Weyland Files, Part 7: Alien Resurrection (1997)
item.description:
Pip and Alder resurrect the black sheep of the Alien films: Jean-Pierre Jeunet and Joss Whedon's Alien Resurrection (1997), the movie that pushes the Alien timeline two centuries past Fury 161, retires Weyland-Yutani to the background, and gives us Ripley 8, Call and the Newborn.

  • Development: From a Newt clone treatment to a Ripley clone; Giler and Hill's cloning idea; Weaver's co-producer credit and reported $11 million salary.
  • The director search: Danny Boyle, Peter Jackson, Bryan Singer, Paul W.S. Anderson and David Cronenberg before Jeunet and his City of Lost Children team (Khondji, Pitof, Perlman, Pinon).
  • Whedon's script: An Earth-set third act, five unused final acts, and a very different bone-white chimera.
  • The shoot: First Alien film made outside England; the 548,000-gallon Stage 16 tank; Winona Ryder's courage; Weaver's real backwards basketball shot.
  • Creatures and design: ADI's swimming xenomorphs, Blue Sky's CGI, the Newborn's nine puppeteers, Nigel Phelps' sets and Sylvain Despretz's Auriga.
  • Score: John Frizzell's romantic, eerie score and the month-long "They Swim" cue.
  • Themes: Cloning and identity, the clone room, twisted motherhood, and Call, the machine more humane than any human.
  • Reception: $47.8M domestic, $161.4M worldwide on a $70M budget; a hit in France and the UK; 56% on Rotten Tomatoes, 63 on Metacritic, CinemaScore B-.
  • The feud: Whedon's "casting is storytelling" critique versus Jeunet's blunt 2022 reply.
  • Special Edition: Bug-squashing opening, Newt nods, the Walmart buyout line, and the ruined-Paris ending shot in snow.
  • Labels: Firefly and Star Trek links as WINKS; Autons as a Blade Runner rhyme (theme, not continuity); human-xeno compatibility via the Engineers as FAN THEORY.
  • Map update: Two centuries after Alien 3 (fan timelines: about 2379-2381); United Systems Military runs xeno research; Weyland-Yutani bought by Walmart (Special Edition only); Autons; Ripley 8 and the Newborn; swimming xenos; a wrecked Earth.

item.title: The Weyland Files, Part 6: Alien 3 (1992)
item.description:
Pip and Alder take on the most argued-about film in the franchise, David Fincher's Alien 3 (1992). They cover William Gibson's "space commies" draft and its later comic, audio and novel lives, Vincent Ward's wooden planet, a shoot that began without a finished script, Giger's return and ADI's first Alien creature, Goldenthal's riot-era requiem, the mystery of Bishop II, the Assembly Cut, and a run of Blade Runner people passing through the Alien films.

  • Development hell: Brandywine first planned a Hicks-led Cold War story. William Gibson was hired in September 1987, followed by Renny Harlin, Eric Red's bio-dome draft, and David Twohy's prison planet. Fox's Joe Roth insisted Ripley return, and Weaver got a reported $4M+, a co-producer credit, and a no-guns story.
  • Gibson's Alien III: The draft has the UPP, Anchorpoint station, and an HIV-like "xenovirus" framed as an ancient bioweapon. It was later adapted as a Dark Horse comic (2018-19, Johnnie Christmas), an Audible drama (2019, Dirk Maggs, with Biehn and Henriksen) and Pat Cadigan's 2021 novel. These are licensed alternate continuity, not on the map.
  • Vincent Ward: Arceon is a wood-and-glass monastery station of technology-hating monks. Jon Landau called it "artsy-fartsy," but much of its DNA (faith, exile, Newt's death, Ripley's death) survived.
  • Production: Shooting started January 14, 1991, at Pinewood with about $7M already spent and no finished script, on a $50-60M budget. Blade Runner's cinematographer Jordan Cronenweth shot about two weeks before illness, and Alex Thomson replaced him.
  • Creature: Giger's "Bambi Burster." Woodruff and Gillis's ADI (recommended by Stan Winston) built the creature, including a 40-inch rod puppet on a bicycle-chain armature. The host is a dog in the theatrical cut and an ox in the Assembly Cut. The host-trait creature is CANON.
  • Score: Elliot Goldenthal spent about a year on it and recorded it during the 1992 LA riots.
  • Themes: Grief; faith among double-Y-chromosome convicts; the AIDS reading (Amy Taubin); and Ripley's chosen death, which denies the Company its Queen.
  • Bishop II: A Weyland-Yutani man who claims to be human and to have designed Bishop (CANON on screen). Being human is the intended reading, per script drafts, the novelization and the Assembly Cut. Being an android is a FAN THEORY. The link to Charles Bishop Weyland (Part 10) is a FAN THEORY based on casting.
  • Box office and reception: $55.47M domestic and $159.81M worldwide per Box Office Mojo. The opening is $19.45M (3-day, Mojo) vs $23.1M (Memorial Day 4-day, Wikipedia). It has 43% on Rotten Tomatoes, 59 on Metacritic and a CinemaScore of C. Siskel and Ebert gave it two thumbs down, and it got an Oscar nomination for Visual Effects.
  • Aftermath: Fincher disowned it (Guardian, 2009), and Cameron called the deaths "a slap in the face." Nolan has praised it. The 2003 Assembly Cut (about 144 minutes, made without Fincher) is often rated higher.
  • Cross-references: Production links only: Cronenweth, Gibson's admiration for Blade Runner (Paris Review via Gizmodo), and ADI leading to the AVP films. The Predator 2 skull (Part 5) is a WINK. No on-screen Blade Runner link.
  • Map update: 2179 (tie-in year). Pins: Fiorina "Fury" 161, a Weyland-Yutani Class C Work Correctional Unit with a lead works and about 25 people; the deaths of Hicks, Newt and Bishop; the runner; Ripley carrying a Queen; Bishop II; a Weyland-Yutani bio-weapons division (tie-ins); and Ripley's death, until Part 7.

item.title: The Weyland Files, Part 5: Predator 2 (1990)
item.description:
The skull episode. Pip and Alder follow the hunter to a sweltering Los Angeles in 1997 and dig into the four seconds of screen time that put Alien and Predator in one universe: the Xenomorph skull in the Predator ship's trophy case. Along the way they cover Arnold's absence, Danny Glover's tired-cop hero, Blade Runner production designer Lawrence G. Paull's "retrograde future" city, the weapons Predator 2 brought into the franchise, the Raphael Adolini pistol that leads to Prey, the NC-17 fight, and Roger Ebert's critique.

  • Development: the Thomas brothers pitched six ideas and Fox picked the "urban jungle." The setting moved from New York to Los Angeles, possibly influenced by Dark Horse's Predator: Concrete Jungle (CREATOR COMMENT from Chris Warner).
  • No Arnold: accounts point to a salary gap (John Davis says $250,000) and, per Stephen Hopkins, James Cameron warning that it would clash with Terminator 2. Swayze, Seagal and Lithgow were all considered at points.
  • Danny Glover: Lt. Mike Harrigan, an "average Joe" hero. Glover took the role to play a Black man fighting a supernatural being.
  • Blade Runner link (CREATOR COMMENT): Lawrence G. Paull, Blade Runner's production designer, described this LA as equal parts Brazil and Blade Runner. It is a design kinship with no continuity claim.
  • City Hunter and arsenal: Stan Winston's redesign, plus the disc, net gun, telescoping combistick and speargun. The Elder's suit was rebuilt from the 1987 Jungle Hunter costume.
  • The skull (CANON): a Xenomorph skull in the trophy case makes the crossover official on screen. Origin stories: Winston artists John Rosengrant and Shane Mahan made it as a nod to Dark Horse's Aliens vs. Predator comic, with Kevin Hudson sculpting, and Hopkins reportedly insisted on keeping it over Fox's objections. The prop was later stolen.
  • Other skulls (FAN THEORY): a humanoid skull that resembles the Space Jockey (Engineer), a four-eyed tyrannosaur-like skull and others, none of them officially identified.
  • Flintlock (CANON): "Raphael Adolini 1715" proves centuries of hunts. Adolini appears in the comic Predator: 1718 and later in Prey (2022). The Elder's 2nd Infantry Division patch hints at Korea (WINK).
  • Ratings and reception: first rated NC-17 and recut for an R. Opened at $8.78M, grossed $57.1M worldwide (Box Office Mojo), 36% on Rotten Tomatoes, 46 on Metacritic, B+ CinemaScore. Kempley was positive, Maslin negative, Ebert gave two stars and argued the film had racial subtext.
  • Theories: Keyes's team studied the 1987 incident (CANON). Harrigan in stasis in the extended cut of Killer of Killers (CANON, extended edition). OWLF as Keyes's agency (FAN THEORY). Predator tech as the seed of Weyland-Yutani (FAN THEORY with a canon endpoint in Requiem). A road from this LA to Blade Runner's LA (Alder's FAN THEORY, about 5%).
  • Unverified: which skull origin story is correct, the four-week shoot figure, "first NC-17 for violence," which Lakers players were in the background, the Tremors sound reuse, and whether "OWLF" appears in the film.
  • Map update: Los Angeles, 1997, the second documented hunt. The Predators have visited Earth for centuries. Their honor code is made explicit. First look at their ship and elders. The Xenomorph skull puts Alien and Predator in one universe (from about 10% to effectively certain). The federal program studying the hunters begins.

item.title: The Weyland Files, Part 4: Predator (1987)
item.description:
Pip and Alder go into the jungle with Predator (1987), the film that brought the second great species into the shared universe. They cover the Rocky joke that started the Thomas brothers' script, the failed Boss Film creature, Stan Winston's six-week redesign (with mandibles suggested by James Cameron), the hard shoot in Mexico, the effects, the score and the reception, then put labels on every theory linking Dutch's hunt to the wider Alien and Predator map.

  • Origins: Jim and John Thomas's first-time script, Hunter, slipped under producer Michael Levy's door and passed to Joel Silver. John McTiernan got the job on the strength of Nomads.
  • The lost Predator: Boss Film's digitigrade, dog-headed red suit and Jean-Claude Van Damme's short time in it. The Hollywood Reporter's oral history gives at least six versions of why he left.
  • Stan Winston: Schwarzenegger recommended him. A Rastafarian painting in Silver's office inspired the dreadlocks, and James Cameron suggested the mandibles (CREATOR COMMENT, and production DNA shared with Aliens).
  • Kevin Peter Hall: the 7'2" performer moved like a dancer in the suit and also played the rescue helicopter pilot. Peter Cullen did the clicking voice.
  • The shoot: Palenque and Puerto Vallarta, a break for Schwarzenegger's wedding, and a second shoot in February 1987 per American Cinematographer. The film is dedicated to two crew members killed in the crash of Mexicana Flight 940.
  • Effects: R/Greenberg's red-suit chroma key with a wider-lens background plate, Inframetrics thermal video and glow-stick blood. Oscar nomination for visual effects.
  • Themes: McTiernan's "we hit nothing" jab at studio gun worship, plus Bibbiani and Monson on masculinity and what it means to be hunted.
  • Score: Alan Silvestri, the only composer to score more than one Alien or Predator film. "Long Tall Sally" comes back in Predators.
  • Box office and reviews: about $15M budget, $12.0M opening and $98.3M worldwide (Box Office Mojo). 65% on Rotten Tomatoes, 47 on Metacritic, B+ CinemaScore. Maslin, Variety and Wilmington were cold, Ebert was warmer.
  • Easter eggs (WINK): the "ugly" line that comes back in Predator 2, Predators and AVP, the Brazilian map used in the briefing, and the Predatoroonops spiders.
  • Theories: Guatemala 1987 (CANON via Predators), Dutch in stasis in the extended cut of Killer of Killers (CANON, extended edition), the claim that the CIA knew about the hunter (FAN THEORY), and Dutch's fight as the first link to Weyland-Yutani's interest in Predator technology (FAN THEORY, with a canon endpoint in Requiem).
  • Unverified: how the Rocky joke's timing fits a 1984 script date, where the Cameron/Winston flight was headed, and the real reason Van Damme left.
  • Map update: 1987 Guatemala, first on-screen contact with the hunters. The species' trophy culture and technology, and the start of its honor code. Dutch survives. No corporate pins yet, so the odds that Alien and Predator share a universe stand at about 10% until next week's skull.

item.title: The Weyland Files, Part 3: Aliens (1986)
item.description:
Pip and Alder go back to LV-426 for James Cameron's Aliens (1986). They cover the lawsuit settlement that funded it, the "Ripley and soldiers" pitch and the dollar-sign title, the troubled Pinewood shoot, Stan Winston's Queen, Syd Mead's Sulaco, Horner's three-week score, the Vietnam and motherhood readings, Bishop, the Special Edition, and why Alder's favorite film is the weakest exhibit in his Blade Runner case.

  • Development: The Brandywine profits suit settled in 1983, with Fox agreeing to finance Alien II. Cameron's November 1983 treatment ran 42 pages per Wikipedia or 45 per TCM, then grew to about 90 during the Terminator delay. The script was finished in February 1985, just before a writers' strike.
  • Deals: Budget offers ranged from Diller's $12M to Fox's $35M estimate, and the film was shot for about $18.5M. Weaver got $1M plus a share of the profits. Cameron confirmed the ALIEN$ pitch story in 2021 (CREATOR COMMENT).
  • Production: Shot at Pinewood and Acton Lane Power Station from September 1985 to January 1986. Dick Bush was replaced by Adrian Biddle, the crew walked out after the first AD was fired, and Michael Biehn replaced James Remar as Hicks.
  • Creatures and design: Stan Winston took over because Giger was committed to Poltergeist II. The Queen is a 14-foot puppet, and about 12 alien suits were used. Syd Mead (Blade Runner's visual futurist) designed the Sulaco, Ron Cobb the dropship, APC and colony, and John Richardson the power loader.
  • Score: Horner had about three weeks. Cameron cut the score up and inserted Goldsmith's Alien cues, and unused material later turned up in Die Hard. The score was still Oscar-nominated.
  • Themes: Cameron's own comments on the Vietnam-era dialogue (via The Take and the Lofficier interview), Ripley and Newt as a mirror of the Queen, Burke as the Company's id, and trauma.
  • Bishop: He prefers "artificial person" and has behavioral inhibitors (CANON). The manufacturer is Hyperdyne Systems. The 341-B model number comes from toys and trading cards (tie-in). The A-B-C-D synthetic naming pattern is a FAN THEORY.
  • Box office and reception: $10.05M opening, $85.16M domestic and $131.06M worldwide per Box Office Mojo. It has 93% on Rotten Tomatoes and 84 on Metacritic, won Oscars for Visual Effects and Sound Effects Editing, and Weaver earned the first Best Actress nomination for a sci-fi film.
  • Special Edition: A 157-minute cut with Amanda Ripley (photo of Elizabeth Inglis), the colony opening and the sentry guns. It is Cameron's preferred version, and Amanda was later picked up by official tie-ins.
  • Creator comments (Starlog, 1987): Cameron explains the Queen's origin, the broken beacon, the gas giant out of frame, and a possible bioweapon mission for the derelict pilot. He also says the creatures' origin is best left unanswered.
  • Cross-references: Weyland-Yutani gets its D and a new logo (CANON). The Predator 2 command-post echo and the Infinity War reference are WINKS. The Syd Mead and Ron Cobb design links are production winks. No verified on-screen Blade Runner link.
  • Map update: 2179 (57 years on screen, the year from tie-ins). Also pinned: LV-426 and Hadley's Hope (a Weyland-Yutani co-financed terraforming colony), the Colonial Marines and Sulaco, Hyperdyne synthetics, and the Queen and hive. Alien: Romulus now sits in the 57-year gap.
