item.title: The Weyland Files, Part 2: Blade Runner (1982)
item.description:
Pip and Alder take on Ridley Scott's Blade Runner (1982): Philip K. Dick's novel, the Fancher and Peoples scripts, a near-collapse of financing, a miserable shoot, failed test screenings, seven versions, the Deckard question, and Alder's first real exhibits for an Alien and Blade Runner shared universe, including the Weyland and Tyrell text hidden on the Prometheus Blu-ray.

  • Development: Hampton Fancher's script optioned in 1977; Michael Deeley recruits Scott, who joins on February 21, 1980; David Peoples rewrites; title bought from William S. Burroughs' treatment of Alan E. Nourse's The Bladerunner.
  • Money: Filmways exits after spending over $2.5 million; Deeley raises $21.5 million in ten days from the Ladd Company/Warner Bros., Sir Run Run Shaw and Tandem Productions.
  • Influences: Hopper's Nighthawks, Metropolis, Hong Kong, Métal Hurlant and The Long Tomorrow by Dan O'Bannon and Moebius, a creative bloodline shared with Alien.
  • Production: Shoot from March 9, 1981; Bradbury Building, Ennis House, Warner backlot; the "T-shirt war"; Scott and Deeley fired but kept working.
  • Craft: Syd Mead's retrofitted city and spinners, Trumbull and Yuricich effects, Jordan Cronenweth's BAFTA-winning photography, Vangelis' synth score, Rutger Hauer's rewritten "tears in rain" speech.
  • Release: June 25, 1982 in 1,290 theaters, about $6.15 million opening against E.T. and The Thing (same day); about $41.8 million worldwide lifetime per Box Office Mojo.
  • Reception: Mixed in 1982 (Sheila Benson's "Blade Crawler", Kael, Ebert), later a Great Movies entry; 89% Rotten Tomatoes, 84 Metacritic; National Film Registry 1993.
  • The seven cuts: Workprint, San Diego sneak, US theatrical, International, broadcast, 1992 Director's Cut (Michael Arick) and the 2007 Final Cut (Charles de Lauzirika, Scott's only full-control version).
  • Deckard question: Scott says replicant (CREATOR COMMENT); Ford and Deeley wanted human; Fancher prefers ambiguity; on screen it depends on the cut.
  • Alien links: PURGE screen shared with Alien's shuttle (WINK); Scott's commentary that this city could support the Alien crew (CREATOR COMMENT); Nostromo Dossier says Dallas worked for Tyrell (tie-in CANON, footnoted); Prometheus UK steelbook text implying Tyrell mentored Peter Weyland (WINK leaning tie-in; no real-world author confirmed).
  • Legacy: 2004 scientists' poll winner per The Guardian, Westwood's 1997 game, K.W. Jeter novels, the "Blade Runner curse" (FAN THEORY, a joke).
  • Map update: November 2019 Los Angeles; Tyrell Corporation and Nexus-6 biological replicants; off-world colonies; replicants outlawed on Earth; a biological (Tyrell) versus mechanical (Weyland) technology fork.

item.title: The Weyland Files, Part 1: Alien (1979)
item.description:
Pip and Alder open The Weyland Files with Ridley Scott's Alien (1979): Dan O'Bannon and Ronald Shusett's script, the Brandywine rewrites that created Ash, the Dune alumni who designed it, Giger's biomechanics, the chestburster, Goldsmith's battle over the score, the box office and the lawsuit that led to Aliens, and the first thin threads tying Alien to Blade Runner.

  • Origins: O'Bannon's unfinished "Memory" pages plus Shusett's B-17 gremlins and implantation ideas became "Star Beast," then Alien, pitched as "Jaws in space."
  • Brandywine: Walter Hill and David Giler wrote about eight drafts and expanded the Ash subplot; the WGA gave O'Bannon sole screenplay credit.
  • Budget: The sources disagree. Wikipedia says a $4.2M budget was doubled; Scott (American Cinematographer, Aug 1979) says a proposed $4.5M settled near $8.5M; Box Office Mojo lists $11M.
  • Design: H. R. Giger (Necronomicon, all creature stages, the derelict, the Space Jockey), Ron Cobb and Chris Foss (the human world), Moebius (space suit concepts), and Carlo Rambaldi on the head mechanics.
  • Influences: The Thing from Another World, Forbidden Planet, Planet of the Vampires, Simak's "Junkyard," Farmer's Strange Relations, and EC Comics.
  • Weyland-Yutani (CANON, with a spelling asterisk): Cobb named "Weylan-Yutani" after British Leyland/Toyota and a Japanese neighbour. The name appears on a monitor and on Aspen beer cans.
  • Score: Scott first wanted Isao Tomita. Goldsmith's cues were re-edited and partly replaced with temp tracks, including Hanson's Symphony No. 2. The score still won the BAFTA.
  • Box office and reception: $84.2M domestic and $109.7M worldwide per Box Office Mojo. Early reviews were mixed; it now has 93% on Rotten Tomatoes and 89 on Metacritic, and it won the Oscar for Visual Effects.
  • Lawsuit: Fox claimed a loss, Brandywine sued, and the 1983 settlement funded a sequel.
  • Blade Runner links: The shared PURGE screen and reused monitor graphics are a WINK. Scott's DVD commentary musing is a CREATOR COMMENT. The "Nostromo Dossier" claim that Dallas worked for Tyrell is a reported WINK. The Prometheus Blu-ray files mentioning Tyrell are teased for Part 13.
  • Theories: The Space Jockey became an Engineer only in retrospect (retcon CANON). Special Order 937 is CANON. The cocoon scene and egg morphing (2003 Director's Cut) are a FAN THEORY with deleted-scene support.
  • Map update: In 2122, per the Colonial Marines Technical Manual, the Nostromo answers the signal. Also pinned: the Company, a hidden synthetic (Ash), the xenomorph life cycle, and the derelict pilot. Blade Runner's 2019 would sit about a century earlier.
